• Common name: Pearlweed
  • Other names: HM, Baby tears, Pearl weed, Manatee mudflower, Amano pearl grass, Pearl grass
  • Scientific name: Hemianthus micranthemoides or Hemianthus glomeratus (conflicting taxonomy)
  • Minimum tank size: 20 litres
  • Lighting: Moderate to high
  • Water hardness: soft to hard (1–20 GH)
  • Substrate: any (can float)
  • Growth rate: moderate to fast
  • Placement: foreground / midground / background
  • Fertilizer: recommended
  • CO2: not needed but recommended
  • Propagation: by clipping mature stems

Hemianthus micranthemoides is often mistaken for Hemianthus callitrichoides, and traders sometimes mix them up. The latter has much smaller foliage.

Many biologists suppose that Hemianthus micranthemoides has been extinct in its native range since 1941. The species found growing abundantly in still waters, wet pools and ditches in Florida is actually Hemianthus glomeratus. At the same time, it is believed that Hemianthus micranthemoides is still widely available in the trade thanks to cultivation in nurseries and gardens. Currently it is not possible to clearly identify Pearlweed, and further research is needed to classify it properly.

The plant is widely available at local fish stores and online. There are two options: the pot variant and the tissue culture variant. The tissue culture variant is lab-grown and safer, as it eliminates the possibility of pest snails and algae. Choose only healthy specimens with an overall bright green appearance and no visible damage.

Before planting, disinfect the stems in a bleach solution to eliminate pest snails, algae and parasites. This is not needed for tissue culture plants: simply remove them from the cup, place them in a bowl of water and rinse off the nutrient gel.
Pearlweed is native to the Mid-Atlantic region of the United States, growing in tidal rivers, preferably in areas with enough water movement and gravel or sandy substrates.

Pearlweed is a bright green, low-growing stem plant suited to different parts of a large, medium or even nano tank. It has small, ovate, narrow, bright green leaves (1 cm long) growing oppositely in whorls of 3–4. The stems are delicate, thin and green, growing upright in low light and forming dense mats under intense light. Under good light and CO2 the leaves release oxygen bubbles (pearling).

The plant can be grown in a variety of tanks, including a nano tank of 20 litres, but it will then need frequent trimming. It is best grown in a tank of at least 40 litres, though under optimal conditions it will fill the tank easily.

Pearlweed is easy to care for and adaptable, but needs trimming from time to time to prevent it overrunning the tank. Its growth depends on nutrients, light intensity and CO2.

Growth rate: until it takes hold it is not a rapid grower. After that, under optimal conditions with high light, it grows so fast that it must be cut back weekly. One plant can carpet a small tank in 2–3 months.

Trimming: without regular pruning the plant grows bushy, which is good for the midground or background. As a foreground plant, the shoots need constant and aggressive pruning with curved scissors to stay short and compact. Heavy trimming promotes dense growth and side shoots, giving a carpet-like look. Pearlweed makes a good carpet but is taller than dwarf baby tears. After trimming, the plant does not look its best for a few days.

Tips for carpeting: if trimmed often, Pearlweed makes runners and forms a carpet. Let them grow to about 5–6 cm and then trim. Putting a clear piece of plastic over the plant lets light through but forces it to grow horizontally. The higher the light, the more the plant creeps instead of growing vertically.

Fertilizing: add liquid fertilizers regularly, such as Easy Green, Brightwell FlorinMulti or Seachem macro- and micronutrients, following the manufacturer's instructions. This keeps the plant healthy and prevents stunted growth and yellowing leaves.

Do routine partial water changes with clean, dechlorinated water weekly and gently vacuum the gravel to remove mulm.

• Temperature: 19–28 °C.
  • pH: adaptable, but optimal 6.5–7.5.
  • Hardness: soft to hard water, 1–15 KH and 1–20 GH.

Lighting: moderate light intensity. Under high light the plant can be used as a carpet, with more compact, bushier growth and many runners. Under low light it grows upward with longer gaps between leaf nodes, and the leaves become darker. For optimal growth and colour, keep the lights on for up to 10 hours daily.

Substrate: any substrate, including sand and gravel; a nutrient-rich substrate is not required.

CO2: not a necessity, as the plant grows in low-tech tanks, but growth is less bushy and dense. With CO2 it looks much better, grows faster and pearls.

Fertilizer: essential. Pearlweed feeds mostly from the water column and its root system is weak, absorbing nutrients mainly through the leaves, so dose liquid fertilizers rather than root tabs.

If you keep shrimp with Pearlweed, note that high CO2 levels and copper (present in most fertilizers) are extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Pearlweed is compatible with a wide variety of aquarium animals: fish (for example bettas, tetras, pearl and honey gouramis, zebra danios, cherry barbs, platies, guppies, Endlers, mollies, otocinclus, pygmy corydoras), snails (Japanese trapdoor, ramshorn, nerite, Malaysian trumpet, black devil snails, Asolene spixi, rabbit snails) and dwarf shrimp (all Neocaridina and Caridina varieties, Amano, ghost, bamboo and vampire shrimp). It provides dense foraging ground and hiding spots for small fish and invertebrates.

Avoid species that may eat it, such as koi, goldfish, oscars, rainbowfish, Jack Dempsey, clown loaches and African cichlids. Unless Pearlweed is kept floating, do not keep it with most crayfish or freshwater crabs, which will cut, eat and uproot plants.

Like most stem plants, Pearlweed is planted by placing healthy stems into the substrate. For pot or tissue culture plants, split the plant into several portions and plant them with aquarium tweezers, placing the delicate stems gently to avoid damage. Some hobbyists use it as a floater in planted and quarantine tanks to create shade, while others grow it as a carpet. It can also be tied to driftwood.

Vegetative propagation is a sure way to multiply it: clip mature stems, form bundles of 2–3 stems and place them in the substrate. Under optimal conditions the parent plants regrow and branch profusely, while the new plants root and sprout new shoots.

Melting: when the plant is moved from emersed to submersed growth it gradually sheds leaves during the first few weeks. This is normal; once settled it takes on the submersed form and grows new leaves.

Leggy bottom leaves: when the plant gets very dense, the bottom leaves yellow and die back from lack of light. Regular trimming prevents this and keeps leaves bright green.

Hard to plant: the root system is poorly developed, so the plant may start floating a few hours after planting. Use small stones to hold it down, or bury the long stems slightly deeper. You can also let it float until ready to plant.

Yellowing leaves: upward growth in dim light and translucent or yellowing leaves can result from high pH or a lack of essential nutrients.

Nitrates and phosphates: the plant depends on nutrients in the water column, and melting can occur when nitrates and phosphates get too low. Dose them regularly.

Benefits:

  • Looks good in jungle-style aquascapes.
  • Versatile: works as a carpet, background plant, floating plant or even in emersed form.
  • Absorbs nitrates, ammonia and phosphates from fish waste, decaying plant matter and tap water.
  • Easy to move or remove, as the roots are thin and delicate.
  • Provides cover and shade for invertebrates and small fish.
  • Offers biofilm, an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.
  • Oxygenates and aerates the water.

Pearlweed spreads vertically and horizontally (via runners) at the same time. It suits beginners, grows in low-tech and high-tech tanks of any size, and its pearling is attractive.
